papers.title: Herbivore and carnivore microbial signatures indicate diet and health variation in human gut microbiota
papers.abstract: Diet is a key factor shaping gut microbiota in mammals, with herbivores and carnivores harboring distinct microbial communities. However, despite humans being highly omnivorous, it remains unclear whether their gut microbiota more closely resembles that of herbivores or carnivores or how individual-level variations along this spectrum are associated with human health status. We compared gut microbiota profiles of 858 samples from 109 mammalian species and constructed a Herbivore-Carnivore (HC) index based on bacterial groups characteristic of each diet. The HC-index positioned humans between herbivores and carnivores and showed that traditional hunter-gatherers and nonhuman apes retained herbivore-leaning profiles, whereas urbanized humans exhibited a shift toward a carnivore-leaning state. By applying the HC-index to >72,000 participants across multiple cohorts worldwide, we found that elevated HC-index values were associated with plant-based and fiber-rich diets, greater microbial diversity, enhanced potential to degrade plant-derived carbohydrates, favorable clinical measures, and lower prevalence of self-reported disease. We demonstrated that the HC balance of gut microbiota captures a conserved diet-related gradient across mammals and provides an interpretable framework linking human diet, microbial function, and health.

papers.title: Preferential recruitment of PML isoform II by incoming HPV16 genome transport vesicles facilitates early stage of infection
papers.abstract: The interplay between promyelocytic leukemia nuclear bodies (PML NBs) and viral infections is complex and multifaceted, with viruses often engaging in a delicate balance of exploitation and evasion of host immune responses. It is well-established that incoming human papillomavirus (HPV) virions associate with PML NBs; however, the mechanism by which HPV targets PML NBs to facilitate early transcription and replication remains elusive. We have shown that HPV genomes are delivered to the nucleus inside membrane-bound vesicles during mitosis and that PML proteins are recruited to HPV-harboring nuclear vesicles prior to egress. Herein, we demonstrate that the PML isoform II (PMLII), but not other PML isoforms, is selectively attracted to incoming HPV still residing in transport vesicles. Using individual PML NB isoform and HPV16 minor protein, L2, over-expression experiments in HeLa cells, we conclude that PML II binds to the lipids of the HPV harbouring membrane-bound vesicles rather than L2. This is in line with previous observations that PML II is the only isoform binding to lipid droplets in the nucleus. We observed that the association of PML NBs with the HPV16 viral genome was transient and lost over time. We also found that nuclear Phospholipase C {beta}4 and {gamma}1 colocalize with PML II-L1 complexes in infected cells. Our data support a model in which PML II contributes to the establishment of early HPV16 infection by organizing host lipid regulatory factors at incoming viral transport vesicles.

papers.title: Chaperone mRNA secondary structure does not strongly track thermal adaptation in bacteria, but groL coding sequence shortens in its disordered C-terminal tail
papers.abstract: Ribosomal and transfer RNAs show clear compositional and structural signatures of adaptation to growth temperature, but messenger RNA does not, and the generality of this asymmetry at individual loci remains untested. We asked whether the two principal bacterial chaperone transcripts, dnaK and groL, encode systematically different mRNA secondary structures in thermophiles relative to mesophiles. Using a phylum-matched cohort of 50 bacterial strains (25 mesophiles, 25 thermophiles; balanced across Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes and Proteobacteria), we folded each coding sequence at 37{degrees}C and 55{degrees}C and compared fifteen thermodynamic and structural descriptors per gene. Raw folding metrics showed no significant group differences after multiple-testing correction. However, after controlling for dinucleotide composition with Altschul-Erickson shuffles, thermophile sequences, particularly groL, retained modestly more residual secondary structure than mesophile sequences. The strongest and cleanest signal was not structural: groL coding sequences are shorter in thermophiles (mean 1626.5 versus 1636.3 nt; Cliff's {delta} = 0.571, P = 5.1x10-4), a relationship that scales continuously with optimal growth temperature and persists after phylogenetic generalised least squares correction (n = 50, Pagel's {lambda} = 0.997, slope = -0.356 nt{degrees}C-1, P = 6.0x10-5). Protein-level alignment localised this difference: approximately three-quarters of the excess deletion signal falls within the terminal ~25 residues corresponding to the intrinsically disordered, glycine/methionine-rich C-terminal tail of GroEL. Thermal adaptation in these loci therefore appears to act primarily on a disordered peptide extension, with only a modest residual signature detectable in mRNA folding after composition is controlled.

papers.title: Tracking the conformational dynamics of single molecules in live cells; GTPase cycling in Cdc42 gradients and microclusters
papers.abstract: The Rho family of GTPases play a critical role in many cellular processes by acting as molecular switches relying on conformational changes to transition between active and inactive states. The spatial distribution and kinetics of these conformational changes are complex and vary across the cell. We describe here biosensors based on environment-responsive fluorescent dyes, capable of reporting the conformational changes of individual GTPase molecules as they traffic within living cells (SPARC Cdc42 and SPARC Rac1, 'Single Particle Activation Reporter Constructs'). We use SPARC Cdc42 to determine the rates of different steps in GTPase regulation, activation/inactivation and membrane insertion, that together generate localized gradients of Cdc42 activity driving cell motility. The biosensors also revealed heterogeneously distributed clusters of Cdc42, the mechanisms of their activation, and potential roles in polarized motility.

papers.title: Establishment of split-TurboID in Plasmodium falciparum facilitates identification of a PfAlba2 protein interaction network during late blood stage development
papers.abstract: Malaria parasites of the genus Plasmodium undergo complex multi-host lifecycles that require precise regulation of gene expression. Unlike model eukaryotes, Plasmodium spp. genomically encodes a limited repertoire of canonical transcriptional regulators, but possess a substantial complement of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), highlighting the importance of post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms in regulating parasite gene expression. Among these RBPs are a family of DNA/RNA-binding proteins termed 'Alba' (acetylation lowers binding affinity) of which six have so far been identified in these parasites. Here, we investigated the localisation, functional importance and molecular associations of P. falciparum Alba protein PfAlba2 using two different endogenously tagged parasite lines. Using a GFP-FKBP tagged line, we demonstrated that PfAlba2 is expressed throughout asexual blood stage development and primarily localised in the cytosol. Conditional mislocalisation experiments indicated that PfAlba2 contributes to normal parasite growth. To overcome challenges in generating a miniTurboID proximity labelling line, we established a custom split-TurboID proximity labelling system for use in P. falciparum to characterise the PfAlba2 proxiome during asexual blood stage development. The split-TurboID system facilitated identification of 101 enriched PfAlba2 proximal proteins in schizont stage development, with significant enrichment for proteins involved in translation initiation, including two additional Alba family members, PfAlba1 and PfAlba4. Complementary RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-seq) identified 380 PfAlba2-associated transcripts with significant enrichments including cytosolic ribosomes, rRNA-processing factors, PfAlba1, and egress and invasion-related transcripts (PfRALP1, PfRON4, PfRH1, PfRH5). Together, these findings implicate PfAlba2 in RNA metabolism and translational regulation, suggesting an important regulatory function for this protein during parasite blood stage development.

papers.title: A Xenopus laevis Model for Systemic Fungal Infections
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis possesses both innate and adaptive immune systems, and we previously demonstrated its utility as an infection model for human bacterial pathogens. In this study, we investigated the utility of X. laevis as a model for fungal infections. The human-pathogenic fungi Candida albicans and Aspergillus fumigatus exhibited greater lethality in X. laevis than the nonpathogenic fungi Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe. In frogs infected with C. albicans, viable fungal cells were detected in the blood and multiple organs early after infection, and gross white lesions and fungal hyphae were observed in the kidneys. C. albicans infection also increased renal expression of the proinflammatory cytokine gene s tnf and il1b, as well as the tissue injury-associated gene clu. Treatment with the antifungal agents amphotericin B and micafungin significantly improved the survival of C. albicans-infected frogs. Furthermore, a homozygous deletion mutant of UME6, a gene associated with C. albicans virulence, exhibited reduced lethality compared with the wild-type strain. These findings establish X. laevis as a vertebrate model of systemic fungal infection that enables the evaluation of fungal virulence, host responses, and the therapeutic efficacy of antifungal agents.

papers.title: Functional characterisation and identification of a core interactome of Plasmodium regulatory protein Alba4
papers.abstract: Plasmodium spp. parasites have complex lifecycles that rely on strict regulation of gene and protein expression. Current evidence suggests that P. falciparum has a relatively limited repertoire of canonical transcriptional regulators and RNA interference (RNAi)-associated small RNAs compared to model eukaryotes, potentially reflecting a greater reliance on RNA binding protein (RBP)-mediated post-transcriptional regulation (PTR). Among these RBPs, the acetylation lowers binding affinity (Alba) family of DNA/RNA-binding proteins has been implicated in RNA metabolism and regulation of mRNA stability and translation. In Plasmodium spp. parasites, the Alba family has expanded to include up to six members, with sequence divergence and structural modifications beyond the conserved Alba domain leading to diversification of family members, some of which appear restricted to Plasmodium and related parasites. In this study, we were unable to truncate PfAlba4, but successfully generated an endogenously tagged PfAlba4 parasite line, representing the first successful instance of endogenous tagging of a PfAlba family protein. Utilising this transgenic line, we confirm ubiquitous expression throughout blood stage development and its predominantly cytosolic localisation. Conditional loss of PfAlba4 through the knock-sideways approach demonstrated an important role for PfAlba4 in blood stage development and proteomics analysis defined a protein interaction network of 67 significantly enriched proteins, with notable enrichment of proteins potentially involved in RNA processing and regulation. Further characterisation of one of these proteins, the uncharacterised protein PF3D7_0706500, revealed a partially overlapping network of proximal proteins enriched for RNA-regulatory factors, suggesting potentially shared roles in PTR. RNA Immunoprecipitation-Sequencing (RIP-seq) identified 692 PfAlba4 associated transcripts, with an enrichment of a pyrimidine-rich motif in their 3' untranslated regions, suggesting a potential sequence-dependent mechanism of RNA recognition. Integration of proteomic and RIP-Seq datasets in late blood stage parasites revealed a consistent association with RNA processing and regulatory pathways, implicating PfAlba4 in post-transcriptional regulation. Together these findings establish PfAlba4 as an important component of the RNA-regulatory landscape in P. falciparum and highlight the importance of PfAlba proteins for malaria parasite blood stage development.

papers.title: NON-NUCLEOSIDE REVERSE TRANSCRIPTASE INHIBITORS BLOCK THE INCORPORATION OF VIRAL GLYCOPROTEINS INTO HIV-1 VIRIONS
papers.abstract: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) are a key component of antiretroviral therapy that block reverse transcription in newly infected cells. NNRTIs have also been reported to induce premature activation of the HIV-1 protease in virus-producing cells, an activity that has been optimized in a class of NNRTIs known as targeted activators of cell kill (TACK). In this study, we used the TACK compound Pyr01 to investigate how NNRTI-induced premature protease activation affects virion composition and infectivity. We found that Pyr01 treatment markedly reduces the incorporation of the HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycoprotein into virus particles in an Env cytoplasmic tail-independent manner. Pyr01 treatment also disrupts the virion incorporation of foreign viral glycoproteins and causes a substantial loss of the viral enzymes from virions. Virions produced from NNRTI-treated cells exhibit reduced membrane order. The defect in viral glycoprotein incorporation requires an active protease, implicating premature protease-mediated disruption of the Gag lattice and resulting changes in membrane properties as the primary mechanism underlying these effects. These findings reveal that NNRTI-induced premature protease activation during virus assembly fundamentally changes the protein composition and membrane order of HIV-1 virions to markedly reduce particle infectivity. These results have implications for the use of TACK compounds therapeutically and provide basic insights into the properties of the viral membrane that promote viral glycoprotein incorporation.

papers.title: Heat-killed Latilactobacillus sakei D279 Attenuates Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Intestinal Inflammation and Barrier Disruption
papers.abstract: Intestinal barrier dysfunction and excessive inflammation contribute to the pathogenesis of various metabolic and gastrointestinal diseases. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induces systemic and intestinal inflammation, disrupts epithelial tight junctions, and impairs intestinal barrier integrity. Although heat-killed Latilactobacillus sakei D279 exhibits antiviral activity, its effects on intestinal barrier function remain unclear. In this study, we examined whether heat-killed D279 preserves intestinal barrier integrity and attenuates LPS-induced inflammatory responses in vivo (LPS-challenged mice), ex vivo (mouse peritoneal macrophages), and in vitro (IEC-6 intestinal epithelial cells). Cytokine and receptor gene expression in macrophages was measured to evaluate inflammatory responses. Furthermore, barrier function was assessed using transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), and the expression of tight junction-related genes was assessed. D279 alleviated LPS-induced intestinal injury in LPS-challenged mice, as indicated by the attenuation of colon shortening and histopathological changes compared to those in the LPS control group. In peritoneal macrophages, D279 pretreatment suppressed LPS-induced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-, IL-1{beta}, and IL-12{beta}), increased IL-10 expression, and reduced LPS-induced upregulation of MLCK expression. This postbiotic increased basal cell viability in a concentration-dependent manner in IEC-6 cells. Moreover, it enhanced epithelial barrier development (increased TEER) and upregulated tight junction gene expression. These findings demonstrate that heat-killed D279 primarily confers its benefits by attenuating LPS-induced cytokine responses, limiting the upregulation of MLCK expression, and partially preserving goblet cell abundance. This is consistent with its protective postbiotic role in intestinal homeostasis. Thus, this study introduces a candidate postbiotic for the promotion of intestinal resilience under systemic inflammatory stress.

papers.title: Surface adhesion-dependent DNA extraction bias points to an 'anvil effect' during mechanical lysis
papers.abstract: DNA extraction bias is usually treated as an intrinsic property of a cell's envelope, size, or physiology rather than a feature of its physical location. Most soil bacteria live attached to surfaces, and attached cells should lyse preferentially during bead-beating if a bead striking a particle crushes the cell against it, as on an anvil, whereas a free cell must be caught between colliding beads. We tested this 'anvil effect' in sterile synthetic soil microcosms using isogenic strain pairs that differ in adhesion in two bacteria with different modes of attachment. Agrobacterium tumefaciens anchors with a unipolar polysaccharide and aggregates in an exopolysaccharide matrix, whereas Caulobacter vibrioides attaches individually by a polar holdfast. Within each strain we calculated the ratio of DNA yield from mechanical to chemical lysis, then compared adherent with non-adherent strains. In support of the anvil effect, mechanical lysis favored adherent cells in A. tumefaciens (2.0-fold) and C. vibrioides (2.6-fold). The route by which soil was transferred to the lysis tube altered the extent of bias observed, further indicating the importance of considering physical context during DNA extraction. Our synthetic soil was standardized and aggregate-free, leaving cells exposed on particle surfaces, making these results a direct test of the anvil effect. In natural soils, the aggregation, texture, and moisture may offset or amplify this effect. Surface attachment therefore biases soil DNA extraction, complicating corrections that treat extraction efficiency as a fixed, strain-specific coefficient.

papers.title: Hyperactivation of Mincle in exacerbated apical periodontitis in an autoinflammatory mouse model for cherubism
papers.abstract: Aims: To examine the role of Mincle, a C-type lectin (Clec) pathogen recognition receptor (PRR), in exacerbated apical periodontitis (AP) in an autoinflammatory mouse model for cherubism (CBM). Methodology: Patients with immune system dysfunction have higher prevalence of AP but the mechanism remains largely unknown. We studied a knock-in (KI) mouse model carrying a Sh3bp2 mutation for CBM. We performed pulp exposure in one lower 1st molar of 5- to 6-week-old mice to introduce pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMP)-induced endodontic infection. We determined the expression levels of Clec subfamily genes by qPCR. To suppress Mincle, we generated Sh3bp2+/+Mincle+/+, Sh3bp2+/KIMincle+/+, and Sh3bp2+/KIMincleKO/KO mice or injected Sh3bp2+/KI mice with a Mincle-binding DNA aptamer (AptMincle). Mice were analyzed 42 days after pulp exposure by micro-CT (mCT), qPCR and immunoblotting. Statistical analysis was performed by one-way ANOVA followed by post-hoc analysis with Tukeys test or two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak correction. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Expression of Clec4e (Mincle) was significantly increased in Sh3bp2 mutant mice after pulp exposure compared to WT littermates (p<0.0001). Sh3bp2+/KIMincle+/+ and Sh3bp2+/KIMincleKO/KO mice had a comparable response to pulp exposure, including the degree of bone loss and induction of inducible NOS (iNOS), IL-1b, and TNF-a. Sh3bp2+/KI mice injected with AptMincle after pulp exposure for 21 days showed significant amelioration of bone loss compared to mice with vehicle injection (p<0.0001). Conclusions: These seemingly conflicting data of suppressing Mincle by crossing with Mincle KO mice and AptMincle injection suggest that Mincle has dual functions upon PAMPs stimulation, consistent with a previous study showing that Mincle enhances tissue destruction during the inflammatory stage and is subsequently needed for inflammation resolution. Fine-tuned suppression of Mincle significantly reduces the severity of AP in Sh3bp2+/KI mice. This study suggests that patients with CBM may benefit from more frequent dental examinations and early intervention to reduce or prevent severe progressive bone loss in periapical tissues.

papers.title: Sphingolipid Hydroxylation Governs Fungal Pathogenicity and Drug Susceptibility: Scs7 as a Druggable Target in Candida albicans
papers.abstract: Sphingolipids are essential structural components of the fungal plasma membrane and key signaling hubs that orchestrate pathogenicity. While both fungi and mammals perform sphingolipid hydroxylation, they rely on evolutionarily divergent enzymatic systems, establishing a biochemical divergence exploitable for selective targeting. Here, through a screening of sphingolipid metabolic genes, we identify the sphingolipid -hydroxylase Scs7 as a central regulator of membrane homeostasis, virulence, and caspofungin susceptibility in Candida albicans. Genetic ablation of SCS7 depletes hydroxylated sphingolipids, disrupts memberane organization, and compromises cell wall integrity, which collectively impair hyphal morphogenesis, biofilm formation, and stress tolerance through blockade of the cAMP-PKA signaling axis. In a murine cutaneous infection model, SCS7 deletion markedly attenuates fungal burden, hyperinflammation, and epidermal barrier disruption, underscoring its non-redundant role in host-pathogen interaction. Leveraging the fungus-specific architecture of Scs7, we performed virtual screening and identified resveratrol as a natural Scs7 inhibitor. Resveratrol recapitulates the lipidomic and phenotypic defects of SCS7 deletion and synergizes with caspofungin to enhance fungal killing. Our study establishes sphingolipid -hydroxylation as a master determinant of fungal membrane fitness and validates Scs7 as a promising, fungus-specific antifungal target with dual anti-virulence and chemosensitizing activities.

papers.title: Evolutionarily distinct dengue virus type 2 with a unique type-specific neutralization determinant
papers.abstract: Dengue viruses 1-4 (DENV1-4) mostly circulate in endemic cycles involving humans and Aedes mosquitoes. However, rare dengue outbreaks originate from non-human primates. These spillovers are caused by sylvatic virus genotypes that are closely related to endemic strains of the same serotype, but some are caused by strains that fall between the four canonical serotypes on phylogenetic trees. It is not clear whether these genotypic differences are reflected in corresponding antigenic differences. Here, we characterized the antigenic features of QML-22, a divergent strain most closely related to DENV2. On an antigenic map, QML-22 clustered with other globally representative DENV2 strains. QML-22 was not as well neutralized by antisera raised against endemic DENV2 and was better neutralized by antisera from DENV1, 3, and 4 infections than other strains of DENV2. QML-22 had a cluster of distinct amino acid residues in domain I of the envelope (E) protein, with only scattered point mutations elsewhere in the envelope. A potently neutralizing anti-DENV2 antibody that targets this site in domain I of the E protein, 3F9, had >1000-fold lower neutralization of QML-22 than other endemic DENV2 strains, whereas other cross-reactive and DENV2-specific antibodies neutralized QML-22 and endemic strains to similar titers. When antisera from non-human primates infected with QML-22 or DENV2 reference strain S16803 were depleted with the heterologous virions, homologous neutralization was unaffected but heterologous neutralization was reduced, suggesting homologous neutralization was due to distinct epitopes. Evolutionary analyses showed the 3F9 epitope was under relaxed selection pressure compared to other neutralizing epitopes and that QML-22 had unique amino acids in this epitope relative to the likely common ancestor of all DENV2. These findings provide insight into the antigenic diversification of DENV and the possible evolution of new serotypes.

papers.title: Accessory B Chromosomes Alter Chromatin Accessibility and Gene Expression in Maize Pollen Nuclei
papers.abstract: B chromosomes in maize (Zea mays L.) are supernumerary, nonessential chromosomes that exhibit non-Mendelian inheritance through chromosome drive. During the second pollen mitosis, they undergo nondisjunction, resulting in their preferential transmission via B-containing sperm cells. Although their transmission mechanisms have been extensively characterized, the effects on chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation in gametophytic cells remain poorly understood. Here, we combined flow cytometric sorting of pollen nuclei with an assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (ATAC-seq) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to investigate the impact of B chromosomes on chromatin accessibility and gene expression in mature maize pollen. Using pollen nuclei isolated from a maize inbred line B73 carrying zero and two B chromosomes, we generated high-purity datasets suitable for integrated chromatin and transcriptomic analyses. We identified extensive chromatin accessibility and transcriptional activity at B-chromosome loci. Importantly, the presence of B chromosomes was also associated with altered chromatin accessibility and gene expression on the standard A chromosomes, revealing regulatory effects extending beyond the B chromosome itself. Together, these findings contribute to a broader understanding of effects of selfish genetic elements in plants.

papers.title: Serum extracellular vesicle proteomics reveals treatment-associated biomarkers in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Background Longitudinal biomarkers of treatment response in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are needed. Extracellular vesicle (EV)-enriched serum proteomics may provide a minimally invasive approach for monitoring systemic and tumor-associated responses to therapy. Methods Paired pre-treatment and post-treatment serum samples were analyzed from 51 patients with pancreatic cancer, including 25 treated with FOLFIRINOX and 20 treated with gemcitabine-based therapy. EVs were enriched using the Mag-Net method and profiled by data independent acquisition mass spectrometry. After batch correction and filtering, 941 proteins were retained for differential and pathway analyses. Paired linear models and gene set enrichment analyses were used to assess treatment-associated changes. Baseline protein abundance and longitudinal changes were evaluated in relation to overall survival (OS) using Cox models. Results A total of 2,089 EV-associated proteins were identified, with an average of 1,186 proteins quantified per sample. Across the cohort, 26 proteins differed between post- and pretreatment samples. Proteins that increased after treatment were primarily related to extracellular matrix organization and cell adhesion, whereas proteins that decreased after treatment were associated with actin cytoskeletal organization, coagulation, and hemostasis. Treatment-associated changes were more pronounced in the FOLFIRINOX group, in which 32 proteins were differentially expressed. FOLFIRINOX was characterized by coordinated reductions in platelet- and coagulation-associated proteins, including PF4, PF4V1, PPBP, GP5, ITGA2B, and ITGB3, accompanied by enrichment of platelet activation, coagulation, and hemostasis pathways among down-regulated processes. No individual proteins met the same significance threshold in the gemcitabine group. A composite seven-protein platelet score decreased significantly after FOLFIRINOX but not for gemcitabine, and the between-regimen difference in score change was significant. Higher pretreatment ITGB1 abundance was associated with longer OS after multiple-testing correction (HR, 0.112; BH-FDR = 0.0063). In multivariable analysis, greater treatment-associated platelet-score depletion was independently associated with shorter OS (HR per unit increase in {Delta}score, 0.56; P = 0.030). Conclusions Longitudinal serum EV-enriched proteomics identified treatment-associated biological changes in PDAC, including a coordinated platelet-related response predominantly observed after FOLFIRINOX. Baseline ITGB1 abundance and longitudinal platelet-score changes represent potentially complementary prognostic and pharmacodynamic markers. These findings are exploratory and require validation in larger, independent cohorts incorporating platelet counts, coagulation measurements, and targeted proteomic assays.

papers.title: PHYLOGENETIC SUPPORT FOR THE EVOLUTION OF APOSEMATISM BEFORE GREGARIOUSNESS IN CONIFER SAWFLIES
papers.abstract: The evolutionary origin of aposematism remains a long-standing puzzle: how can a conspicuous mutant persist and spread within a cryptic prey population? Two competing hypotheses have been proposed. The group-first hypothesis suggests that aposematism evolved secondarily in already aggregating, chemically defended cryptic ancestors, whereas the aposematism-first hypothesis suggests that aposematism arose in solitary ancestors, with gregariousness evolving subsequently. Currently, these two evolutionary pathways have only been studied in caterpillars of Lepidopteran species, but we lack wider taxonimical evidence especially from systems with cryptic but chemically defended species. We evaluated these hypotheses using phylogenetic reconstructions in chemically defended conifer sawflies (Hymenoptera: Diprionidae), a group whose larvae vary in both colouration and aggregation behaviour. Almost half the species examined (20/45) had aposematic and gregarious larvae. Aposematism and gregariousness were positively evolutionarily correlated (r = 0.29). Aposematic and gregarious species tended to evolve from aposematic, solitary ancestors, while species with cryptic and gregarious larvae (14/45) tended to evolve from aposematic and gregarious ancestors, a pattern consistent with the aposematism-first hypothesis.

papers.title: Within-host evolution of an avirulent Salmonella vaccine strain reveals regulatory tuning of virulence functionality without loss of function
papers.abstract: Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) relies on a costly epithelial invasion program encoded in Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 (SPI-1) to overcome microbiota-mediated colonization resistance. Because SPI-1 expression is a cooperative trait in which a minority of invasive SPI-1ON cells benefits the wider bacterial population, inflammatory infection models readily select for permanently avirulent "cheater" mutants defective in SPI-1 function. However, while frequently observed during acute infection, isolates from persistent human NTS infection rarely exhibit obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function mutations, raising the question of whether SPI-1 contributes to bacterial fitness beyond induction of acute intestinal inflammation and tissue persistence. Here, we addressed this question using a metabolically attenuated yet epithelial-invasive auxotrophic Salmonella serovar Typhimurium (STm) vaccine strain (STmAux) that persistently colonizes the murine intestine without causing overt inflammatory pathology or tissue infection while retaining SPI-1-dependent host interaction and immunogenicity. Following within-host evolution for up to five years, STmAux populations did not accumulate classical hilD or other obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function cheater mutants. Instead, parallel evolution repeatedly targeted the BarA/SirA two-component regulatory system, closely mirroring previous observations in persistent human NTS infections. Functional analyses demonstrated that evolved barA and sirA alleles tune rather than abolish SPI-1 function by sharply reducing the proportion of SPI-1ON cells while preserving their individual epithelial invasion competence. Reconstructed in a prototrophic strain background, early evolved isolates retained full intestinal and systemic virulence in vivo despite exhibiting strongly reduced SPI-1ON frequencies in vitro. Remarkably, identical sirA mutant alleles also emerged in a hilD-deficient strain background, indicating that selection for these adaptive variants is not contingent on canonical HilD-dependent SPI-1 activation. During prolonged evolution, additional mutations accumulated that were associated with loss of systemic virulence despite preservation of epithelial invasiveness, suggesting subsequent adaptation affecting host-interaction pathways beyond SPI-1-mediated virulence. Together, these findings identify regulatory tuning of the BarA/SirA control network as a conserved evolutionary trajectory during prolonged NTS persistence. Rather than favoring classical cheater-driven loss of virulence functions, long-term adaptation preserves substantial SPI-1-dependent host interaction while reducing the proportion of phenotypically virulent SPI-1ON cells.

papers.title: Structural signatures of salinity adaptation in Microviricetes capsids
papers.abstract: Phages, like their bacterial hosts, have evolved to proliferate across the full range of environments on Earth, but the specific amino acid residues that underlie their environmental adaptations remain elusive. Here, we developed a computational framework that uses structure-based multiple sequence alignments, a random forest classifier, and a phylogeny-aware regression model to find amino acid residues linked to specific environments. Applying this framework to public metagenomic data, we analyzed 1,110 Microviricetes major capsid proteins (MCPs) from the lake and ocean biomes, and found that ocean virus capsids were highly enriched in negatively charged residues on internal and external surfaces. This adaptation likely helps maintain solubility at high salt concentrations and stabilizes ssDNA-capsid interactions by sequestering positively charged ions inside the capsid. At intersubunit interfaces, ocean capsids showed enrichment of cation-{pi} and {pi}-{pi} interactions, which are more resistant to solvation than salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Amino acid residues in lake capsids were more often substituted by biochemically dissimilar amino acids in ocean capsids than the reverse. Together, these results show that microvirus capsids adapt to high-salt environments through changes in surface charge and substitutions affecting intersubunit interactions. Further, we describe a general approach for studying the adaptation and stability of any protein family under complementary environmental or phenotypic conditions.

papers.title: A proteomics screen of HIV-1 ASP interactors reveals multifaceted effects on host cell homeostasis
papers.abstract: Nearly four decades after the identification of the HIV-1 antisense gene asp, the function of its protein product remains unclear. Evidence of ASP expression in vivo and the high degree of conservation of the asp gene among pandemic HIV-1 strains suggest a beneficial role for the virus. Using a mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics screen for ASP interactors, we identified nuclear, cytosolic, and mitochondrial host factors, congruent with variable sub-cellular ASP localization. A majority of the host factors identified in the MS screen are involved in pathways essential for host cell homeostasis, including DNA damage repair, intracellular protein transport, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Validating the biological relevance of these findings, we demonstrate that ASP shuttles to the nucleus to promote DNA damage repair and cell viability in response to genotoxic stress. We also finds that ASP promotes translation of mitochondrially encoded host proteins involved in cellular respiration and contributes to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential. Together, these studies identify ASP as a modulator of two major pathways of cellular homeostasis in infected cells, which has direct implications for HIV-1 persistence, spread, and the long-term survival of the viral reservoir.

papers.title: Genotype-Informed Drosophila Kinome Screening Prioritizes PRKX as a Candidate Vulnerability in Bladder Cancer
papers.abstract: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer is molecularly heterogeneous, and the basal/squamous subtype frequently exhibits elevated EGFR expression and TP53 and RB1 alterations. Functional vulnerabilities associated with these alterations remain incompletely defined, while large-scale in vivo screening in mammalian models is experimentally demanding. Therefore, we developed a genotype-defined Drosophila melanogaster model combining Egfr overexpression, mutant p53, and Rbf suppression in Malpighian tubules. The resulting 3-hit model showed increased Malpighian tubule volume and reduced adult eclosion rate. A dominant modifier screen targeting 216 kinase genes identified 72 genes whose perturbation significantly increased the eclosion rate, and a complementary RNA interference screen identified eight kinases whose knockdown increased the eclosion rate. Among these hits, Pka-C3, which is a Drosophila ortholog of human PRKX, emerged as one of the strongest suppressors of the 3-hit phenotype. PRKX was prioritized for further study because public transcriptomic datasets showed higher PRKX expression in bladder tumors than in normal bladder tissue. PRKX knockdown reduced spheroid volume in four human bladder cancer cell lines with distinct EGFR, TP53, and RB1 profiles. Both small interfering RNAs produced significant reductions in two cell lines, whereas only one siRNA reached significance in the other two. These findings nominate PRKX as a candidate vulnerability in bladder cancer and highlight a cross-species approach that combines genotype-informed Drosophila screening with functional testing in human cancer cells to prioritize targets for further investigation.

papers.title: The Phospholipase A2 Activity of Peroxiredoxin 6 Protects Hepatocarcinoma Cells Against Ferroptosis and Mitophagy Impairment
papers.abstract: Peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6) is a moonlighting protein that plays a key role in regulating redox homeostasis and lipid metabolism through its unique dual peroxidase and calcium-independent phospholipase A2 (iPLA2) activities. Here, we generated a stable HepG2 cell line harboring a D140A mutation to selectively ablate iPLA2 activity, and we compared its phenotype with that of wild-type (WT) and PRDX6-knockout (KO) cells. D140A exhibited low ROS leves, similar to WT cells, confirming that oxidative stress is due to peroxidase deficiency. In contrast, D140A cells displayed higher lipid peroxidation than WT cells, though significantly lower than that of KO cells. Furthermore, the D140A mutant mirrored the KO phenotype regarding intracellular ferrous iron accumulation, impaired lipid droplet biogenesis, and the downregulation of the key ferroptosis regulator GPX4. Mechanistically, integrated proteomic, lipidomic, and enzymatic analyses revealed that a deficiency in iPLA2 activity of PRDX6 disrupted the release of key lipid species necessary for cell structure and signaling. Consequently, organelles involved in lipid synthesis and trafficking, such as peroxisomes, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and lipid droplet, were affected. Specifically, we found that mitochondria exhibited a reduction in cristae and a diminished capacity for mitophagy and autophagy, which ultimately makes cells much more susceptible to erastin-induced ferroptotic cell death. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that PRDX6 iPLA2 activity uniquely coordinates organelle lipid homeostasis and mitophagy to protect cancer cells from ferroptotic cell death. Consequently, the use of iPLA2 inhibitors such as MJ33, which decreased PRDX6 iPLA2 activity to a level comparable to the mutant D140A, could represent a promising therapeutic strategy for inducing ferroptotic cell death in hepatocellular carcinoma.

papers.title: TaxaAudit: A statistical model of consensus in phylogenetics identifies non-monophyletic taxa
papers.abstract: Interpreting variation in genes and traits across species requires understanding their evolutionary relationships. Taxonomic hierarchies provide a practical approximation of the tree of life, with the NCBI taxonomy linking this framework directly to public sequence data. Some named groups, however, are not evolutionary clades, and recognizing these exceptions requires knowledge scattered across the phylogenetics literature. Here we introduce TaxaAudit, a statistical model that identifies taxonomic groups whose monophyly is repeatedly contradicted by published phylogenies. The model accounts for background taxonomic conflict and the ability of each study's species sampling to expose non-monophyly. Applied to 5,865 molecular phylogenies from TimeTree, TaxaAudit flagged 516 NCBI taxa at family rank and below for significant recurrent contradiction of monophyly. Excluding these taxa's monophyly requirements improved the taxonomy's agreement with independent phylogenomic reference trees and phylogenies withheld from discovery. Flagged taxa were also 3.61 times as likely as matched controls to have their monophyly challenged in publications outside the discovery set. In tree-inference experiments, excluding these monophyly constraints improved agreement with reference phylogenies relative to enforcing the unmodified taxonomy. By identifying groups whose monophyly should not be assumed, TaxaAudit lets researchers draw on published phylogenetic knowledge without reviewing the specialist literature for every taxon. This supports broader use of the NCBI taxonomy as an evolutionary framework for biological comparisons.

papers.title: Caregiver genotype influences larval body size in ants by modulating ecdysteroid production
papers.abstract: Parental genes shape the offspring's rearing environment and, consequently, offspring phenotypes. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these indirect genetic effects remain largely unknown. Here, using the clonal raider ant Ooceraea biroi, we uncover a neurohormonal mechanism by which caregiver genotypes affect larval body size and caste fate. Larval transcriptomics revealed caregiver-genotype effects on neuropeptides and an ecdysteroid biosynthesis gene, while enrichment analyses implicated changes in lipid metabolism. We found that the receptors of these candidate neuropeptides are expressed in the prothoracic gland, the site of ecdysteroid synthesis, and pharmacological manipulations revealed a neuropeptide-ecdysone axis that regulates body size in ants. The same hormonal axis also regulates multiple lipid-binding carrier protein genes expressed in larval fat-body cells. Together, we identify a neurohormonal pathway that is modulated by caregivers in developing larvae, linking lipid metabolism, systemic growth, and caste development.

papers.title: Beyond tree-like evolution in ostariophysan fishes
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic trees have long been a powerful model of the evolutionary history. However, key processes in speciation, such as introgression and hybridization are difficult to depict with strictly binary trees alone, even with modern discordance metrics and post-hoc tests. Phylogenetic networks offer an intuitive way to estimate and interpret these reticulate events, as conflicting signal from gene trees should become evident as hybrid edges. Phylogenetic networks raise a number of challenges over tree-based analyses though, including the estimation of uncertainty and evaluating confidence among multiple competing network hypotheses. Here, we develop a new approach for assessing branch and topological support on networks using composite likelihood, and explore the utility of such statistics by revisiting competing evolutionary hypotheses in ostariophysan fishes. Our results suggest that a tree-like topology is not the best model for ostariophysans. A phylogenetic network with four reticulation events involving early-diverging lineages was the best alternative scenario. Our branch support metrics demonstrated non-negligible levels of uncertainty in the placement of those reticulation events though. An important question though, is if the uncertainty in the placement of these reticulation edges affects the qualitative conclusions of organismal evolution. To this end, we apply our network hypotheses to the biogeographic history of ostariophysans. Since no biogeographic models for networks exist, we implemented a parsimony approach using Fitch's algorithm for ancestral character state reconstruction. This represents the first biogeographic reconstruction for networks, and while simplistic, is a basis for further development. Biogeographic results are generally consistent with previous research on the presence of ancestral lineages in Laurasia and Gondwana post the break-up of Pangea, but also identify some cases of long-distance dispersal.

papers.title: Cxcr2 is required for ductal outgrowth and shapes the stromal microenvironment in postnatal mammary gland development
papers.abstract: Mammary gland development requires coordinated signaling between epithelial and stromal compartments. While CXC chemokine receptor 2 (CXCR2) is known to regulate inflammatory and tissue remodeling processes in disease, including breast cancer, its role in mammary gland morphogenesis is not well understood. Here, we examined postnatal mammary gland development in germline Cxcr2 knockout mice. Loss of Cxcr2 resulted in delayed ductal outgrowth, reduced epithelial area, and altered stromal architecture, including decreased adipocyte size and increased collagen deposition, despite preserved branching organization. These defects occurred in the context of severe systemic immune dysregulation, marked by expansion of granulocytic populations and loss of adaptive immune cells. Together, our findings indicate that CXCR2 indirectly regulates mammary gland development through coordination between the epithelium and stroma, rather than acting through epithelial cell-intrinsic mechanisms. Because the same myeloid expansion, immune suppression, and collagen-rich stromal remodeling that CXCR2 controls during normal development are hallmarks of the pro-tumorigenic breast microenvironment, these findings establish CXCR2 as a regulator of the immune and stromal landscape of the mammary gland and provide a developmental framework for understanding its contributions to the breast tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: An architectural RNA builds a reaction crucible through molecular concentration and activated enzyme selection
papers.abstract: Architectural RNAs (arcRNAs) scaffold membraneless organelles (MLOs), yet how they organize functional proteins remains unclear. Nuclear stress bodies (nSBs), MLOs scaffolded by HSATIII arcRNAs, incorporate SRSFs during stress. During stress recovery, nSBs function as reaction crucibles that recruit the kinase CLK1 to accelerate SRSF rephosphorylation and normalize stress-induced splicing. Here, we identify the ASAP complex as a recruitment factor that recognizes Ser341-phosphorylated, catalytically activated CLK1. HSATIII-bound SRSFs recruit ASAP, assembling a platform for CLK1 recruitment. Biochemical reconstitution reveals that this platform enhances SRSF phosphorylation by concentrating SRSFs and CLK1 while selectively recruiting activated CLK1, establishing nSB reaction crucibles as molecular concentrators and selectors. The SRSF-ASAP-CLK1 interaction network is conserved between humans and mice, suggesting that primate-specific HSATIII arcRNAs co-opted this pre-existing network to establish reaction-crucible function in nSBs. Our findings reveal how arcRNAs organize functional proteins through quantitative enrichment and qualitative selection to build biochemically active MLOs.

papers.title: Moderately acid-tolerant Nitrospira strains obtained by single-colony isolation on plates
papers.abstract: Nitrospira are difficult to cultivate, and pure cultures are mainly obtained by dilution-to-extinction combined with other methods, a process that usually takes years to over a decade. Here, we isolated three Nitrospira strains from activated sludge and sediment within one year using conventional single-colony isolation. Pure cultures of two strains could grow and reform single colonies within 25-60 days on all three types of plates prepared with agar, agarose, and gellan gum. Phylogenetic and phylogenomic analyses placed them within lineage I and indicated that they represent potential novel species, with the provisional names Nitrospira monocolonialis for strain Z02 and Nitrospira limosa for strains Z47 and Z70. All three strains were moderately acid-tolerant, with a minimum tolerable pH of 5.0; strain Z02 showed the highest acid tolerance, retaining 74% of its activity at pH 5.5. Strain Z02 was also highly adaptable to oxygen concentrations of 1-21%, retaining 78% and 85% of its maximum growth rate at 1% and 21% O2, respectively. Compared with the representative lineage I strain Nitrospira defluvii, all three strains contain superoxide dismutase encoding genes and some unique genes. Comparative transcriptomic analysis suggested that strain Z02 upregulated genes involved in stress responses, cell envelope modification, and putative type IVa pilus systems under acidic condition. Overall, this study provides the first demonstration that Nitrospira can grow on plates prepared with common gelling agents and form single colonies within a short period, and that Nitrospira can also tolerate moderately acid conditions.

papers.title: Development of a core genome Multilocus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) and Life Identification Number (LIN) code schema for the Burkholderia cepacia complex
papers.abstract: Background The Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) currently comprises over 20 closely related species; however, understanding Bcc population biology is complicated due to the continual advances in taxonomy and diversity driven by extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Whilst there are conventional typing schemes for the Bcc, including Multilocus Sequence Typing (MLST), there remains a gap for fine-scale resolution typing of the species complex. Here, we present a 1,925 loci core genome MLST (cgMLST) and 14-digit Life Identification Number (LIN) barcoding scheme for the Bcc, that is embedded in the PubMLST database (https://PubMLST.org/organisms/burkholderia-cepacia-complex). Methods A dataset of 142 complete Bcc genomes spanning 19 species were downloaded from NCBI to develop the draft cgMLST scheme (Dataset 1). Two pangenome tools (PIRATE and PEPPAN) were then combined to give a consensus core gene list from Dataset 1. The 'core genes' from these outputs were then screened against the PubMLST loci, using a sequence tag scan, to identify their presence and curate new alleles. The core genes were then validated using a larger Bcc dataset (n = 934 genomes; 22 species) on PubMLST, which had been filtered for high-quality ([≤]200 contigs and 100% ribosomal MLST confidence). This refined the core gene list, ensuring a robust and reliable scheme using a threshold of 99% to classify the gene as 'core'. The population structure of the Bcc was subsequently analysed using the validation dataset to identify genetic clusters using ReporTree. Combined with statistical analysis, 14 allelic mismatch thresholds were identified for the LIN codes. Results The Bcc cgMLST scheme consists of 1,925 loci, which have been designated an arbitrary 'BCC' identifier. The cgMLST scheme and 14-threshold LIN code has been implemented in PubMLST and are publicly available for use. The Bcc genomes in the PubMLST database have been assigned cgSTs and LIN codes. Use cases of the LIN codes were validated using three previously published datasets, which spanned both outbreak investigation and phylogenomic lineage structures. Conclusions This stable, hierarchical LIN code nomenclature enhanced the ability to cluster isolates at multiple levels of resolution with examples overlayed on published datasets provided. The LIN code system is also backwards compatible with previous MLST and clonal complex (CC) nomenclature. Overall, the updated typing scheme will facilitate improve global public health through surveillance of the Bcc epidemiology including source tracing and outbreak investigation

papers.title: BryoCAD: Extending Plant DNA Foundation Models Beyond Flowering Plants
papers.abstract: Bryophytes exhibit diverse genome architectures and gene repertoires, yet their functional interpretation remains constrained by incomplete genomic annotations and limited experimental resources. Although DNA foundation models offer promising solutions, their applicability to evolutionarily divergent bryophytes remains largely unexplored. Here, we introduce BryoCAD, a DNA language model developed through continued pre-training of the angiosperm-specific PlantCAD2 model on 17 bryophyte genomes spanning hornworts, liverworts, and mosses. Across three representative bryophyte genomes and four gene-boundary motif recovery tasks, BryoCAD-Small improved mean zero-shot accuracy from 45.7% to 57.0%, a 24.8% relative increase over PlantCAD2-Small, while the over 200-fold larger Evo2-20B achieved a mean accuracy of only 39.3%. Remarkably, BryoCAD-Small outperformed PlantCAD2-Large in 11 of 12 motif-recovery comparisons across the three bryophytes, highlighting the benefits of lineage-specific adaptation over model scaling alone. These improvements extended to all six tested algal species, increasing mean accuracy from 26.3% to 37.5%, although performance varied across ferns and gymnosperms. BryoCAD also enhanced gene structure annotation: replacing PlantCAD2-Small with BryoCAD-Small increased transcript-level F1 scores from 0.578 to 0.625 in Marchantia polymorpha and from 0.485 to 0.530 in Physcomitrium patens. Together, our findings demonstrate that lineage-specific continued pre-training enhances genomic sequence interpretation and gene annotation across bryophytes, providing a transferable framework for extending DNA foundation models to evolutionarily diverse, understudied plant lineages.

papers.title: Ocean current models predict spatial structure for coastal biodiversity
papers.abstract: Genomic diversity provides the raw material through which all evolutionary processes occur. Accurately describing how environmental features affect patterns of diversity shows promise in predicting the resilience of populations and entire communities to dynamic environments and novel stressors. Identifying the contribution of purely neutral responses to environmental effects can be difficult, especially across large spatial ranges with many covarying environmental features. Using an individual-based model of larvae carried by ocean currents, we predict patterns of neutral genomic diversity in a passively dispersed coastal species, suggesting large geographic regions of relative homogeneity with ancestry determined by the nearest "upstream" population with limited larval input. The genomic identity that dominates each region sharply transitions at the next such interruption, generating hierarchical structure and violating assumptions of isolation-by-distance. We call these upstream populations "lineage source regions" (LSRs), and we find strong concordance between LSR model predictions and an empirical population genomic survey of a keystone salt marsh mussel (Geukensia demissa). We quantitatively validate model performance and goodness-of-fit, updating baseline predictions of genomic diversity patterns from the classic isolation-by-distance model to this LSR framework. This spatially explicit coastal ancestry model has potential for generalization across passive dispersing species.
